questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The thrust a masonry arch contains
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a masonry arch is described as containing a thrust

stimulus.body: The working note below records the evidence for a claim about the thrust a masonry arch contains. thrust is the sideways component of the load that the arch delivers into its supports. A marginal reminder adds: name the sideways push the arch sends into its supports. A reader must decide which of the four proposed statements the note warrants, without using outside knowledge.

questions.stem: With “Explain why a masonry arch is described as containing a thrust / Name the sideways push the arch sends into its supports. / The…” settled, which choice remains consistent with the text?

answer.exemplar: An arch does not carry its load straight down to the ground. The wedge-shaped blocks press on one another and turn the weight into a line of compression that runs around the curve, but that line ends by pushing sideways into the two abutments. That sideways push is the thrust, and it is the reason an arch needs heavy, stiff supports rather than a simple wall below.

questions.explanation: Thrust is the sideways component of the load that the arch delivers into its supports. A freestanding arch has nowhere to send it unless the abutments supply the mass.
questions.hint: Name the sideways push the arch sends into its supports.

stimulus.body: A short reference note on a free arch span with no buttress behind it is set for a close-reading task. It states: The weight of the haunches and any tie must balance the thrust exactly. A marginal reminder adds: explain how the sideways push is held in balance. Four statements are then offered, and only one of them follows from what the note actually says.

questions.stem: The question turns on what the note above shows about a free arch span with no buttress behind it. Given the proposal "Explain how the sideways push is held in balance", which choice is consistent with the evidence in the passage?

answer.exemplar: A free arch has no massive support behind it, so the sideways thrust it generates at the springing has nothing to absorb it. The designer answers by thickening the haunches so their own weight pulls the curve back into equilibrium, or by tying the two supports together with a concealed tie, or by proposing a pointed profile whose thrust is smaller for the same span.

questions.explanation: The weight of the haunches and any tie must balance the thrust exactly. Without that balance the springing feet spread and the arch hinges, dropping the crown.
questions.hint: Explain how the sideways push is held in balance.

questions.topic: The column grid of a hypostyle hall
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a column grid is read as a statement about space

stimulus.body: The working note below records the evidence for a claim about the column grid of a hypostyle hall. a uniform, repeated grid makes the space itself the object of attention. A marginal reminder adds: say what the uniformity of the grid makes the eye read. A reader must decide which of the four proposed statements the note warrants, without using outside knowledge.

questions.stem: Testing “Explain why a column grid is read as a statement about space / Say what the uniformity of the grid makes the eye read. / The…” against the excerpt, which option is the defensible one?

answer.exemplar: The columns are identical, evenly spaced, and run without interruption across the whole hall, so no single column is more important than any other. Because the grid is uniform, the eye stops reading the columns as objects and begins to read the space they define. The hall is thereby presented as one continuous field rather than as a set of privileged bays, and that field is what carries the sacred weight.

questions.explanation: A uniform, repeated grid makes the space itself the object of attention. The supports are deliberately undifferentiated so that the hall can be read as a single field.
questions.hint: Say what the uniformity of the grid makes the eye read.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The load path of a barrel vault
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a vault-carrying wall must be thicker than an ordinary wall

stimulus.body: Read this source excerpt carefully: The vault delivers a horizontal component of load into the wall. A marginal reminder adds: say what extra force the wall must take from the vault. It is followed by four candidate interpretations, of which exactly one is supported by the wording of the excerpt.

questions.stem: The prompt gives “Explain why a vault-carrying wall must be thicker than an ordinary wall / Say what extra force the wall must take from the vault.…” as the nudge. Which option is really supported?

answer.exemplar: A barrel vault pushes outward as well as down, so the wall that springs it has to take a sideways thrust from the vault as well as its own weight. A plain wall is sized only for the load above it and for its own stability, but a vault-carrying wall must also be stiff and massive enough to hold that thrust without moving. Thickening the section is the cheapest way to add the weight and breadth needed to resist the push.

questions.explanation: The vault delivers a horizontal component of load into the wall. A thicker section supplies the mass and stiffness needed to resist that push.
questions.hint: Say what extra force the wall must take from the vault.
